title: Valid Palindrome
directAnswer: Ignore everything that isn't a letter or digit, compare case-insensitively, and check the string reads the same forwards and backwards. The interview-grade answer is two pointers from both ends that skip non-alphanumeric characters in place — O(n) time, O(1) space. The 'clean a new string then reverse' version is fine to mention but uses O(n) extra space.

remember.pattern: Two pointers from both ends, skip non-alphanumeric
remember.formula:
l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
while l < r:
    while l < r and not s[l].isalnum(): l += 1
    while l < r and not s[r].isalnum(): r -= 1
    if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower(): return False
    l += 1; r -= 1
return True
rules: Compare **alphanumeric only** — letters AND digits, not just letters.
Lowercase (or uppercase) both characters before comparing — `'A'` must equal `'a'`.
Guard every inner skip loop with `l < r` so pointers never cross past each other.
Two pointers in place is **O(1) space**; building a cleaned string is O(n) — say which one you're doing and why.
An empty string (or one with no alphanumeric chars) is a valid palindrome → return `true`.
whenToUse: Check symmetry / mirror property of a sequence
Compare characters from both ends inward with a filter
Any 'reads the same backwards' question on strings or arrays
You want O(1) extra space instead of cleaning into a new buffer
antiSignals: Need to find the longest palindromic substring → expand-around-center / DP, not a single scan
Allowed to remove at most k characters → DP or greedy two-pointer with a branch
Linked list palindrome → reverse second half with fast/slow pointers
remember.takeaway: Opposite-end two pointers with an in-place skip is the canonical O(1)-space palindrome check. The same skeleton powers Valid Palindrome II, Reverse String, and the merge step of Two Sum II — recognise it whenever you compare a sequence against its mirror.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can filter characters in place with two pointers instead of allocating a cleaned copy, and whether you remember digits count as alphanumeric and the compare is case-insensitive.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Only skipping letters (forgetting digits), comparing without lowercasing, or dropping the `l < r` guard inside the skip loops so the pointers run off the ends.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the O(n)-space clean-and-compare version, then improve to in-place two pointers for O(1) space. Call out that 'alphanumeric' includes digits and that the comparison is case-insensitive.

problemStatement:
A phrase is a **palindrome** if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome, or `false` otherwise. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers.
constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters
understanding: Strip out punctuation, spaces, and symbols; treat upper and lower case as equal; then ask whether the remaining letters-and-digits sequence is a mirror of itself. We don't build the cleaned string if we don't have to — two pointers can skip the junk on the fly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do digits count, or only letters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Digits count. 'Alphanumeric' = letters and numbers, so "0P" is not a palindrome but "121" is.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the comparison case-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — convert to a single case first. 'A' and 'a' must be treated as equal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about an empty string or one with only symbols?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: After filtering it becomes empty, and an empty string reads the same both ways → return true.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I allocate a new cleaned string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: You can, and it's simplest, but it costs O(n) space. In-place two pointers gets the same answer in O(1) extra space.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: After filtering and lowercasing it becomes "amanaplanacanalpanama", which is a palindrome.
Filtered to "raceacar", which is not a palindrome (first 'r' vs last 'r' ok, but 'a' vs 'a'… 'c' vs 'c'… eventually 'e' vs 'a' mismatch).
Only a space, which is non-alphanumeric. The filtered string is empty, and an empty string is a palindrome.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Two pointers in place is the default; clean-and-compare only when O(n) space is acceptable and clarity matters more.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Clean Then Compare With Reverse
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first — it's the most readable translation of the definition and a fine baseline before optimizing space.
hints: The definition literally tells you the transformation: drop non-alphanumeric characters and lowercase the rest. What's the simplest data structure to hold the result?
Build a new string (or list) of just the lowercased alphanumeric characters.
A string is a palindrome iff it equals its own reverse. Compare the cleaned string to its reverse and return the boolean.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to filter (O(n)) plus one pass to compare with the reverse (O(n)) = O(n) time. The cleaned copy holds up to n characters → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the definition directly: walk the string once, keep only characters where `isalnum()` is true, and lowercase each as you go into a fresh buffer. Then test whether that buffer equals its reverse.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem statement *is* an algorithm: 'convert uppercase to lowercase, remove non-alphanumeric, then check it reads the same both ways.' Building the cleaned string mirrors those words one-to-one, so it's almost impossible to get the logic wrong — which is exactly why it's a good baseline to state out loud.

**Why it's still O(n) and correct.** Filtering is a single linear scan, and comparing a string to its reverse is another linear scan. Both are O(n), so the time is optimal. The only blemish is the O(n) buffer.

**Why we don't ship this.** With `n` up to `2 × 10⁵` the extra string is harmless in practice, but the interviewer is probing whether you can avoid the allocation entirely. Allocating a second copy when two indices would do is the thing to improve — so mention this, then pivot to two pointers.
approaches.insight: Reversing-and-comparing is the most literal encoding of 'reads the same backwards'. It's correct and O(n) time — the only thing wrong with it is the O(n) space, which is precisely the door the interviewer wants you to open toward two pointers.

[::-1] reverses the list; equality checks the palindrome property.

pitfalls: Filtering only letters (Character.isLetter) and dropping digits — '0P' would wrongly pass.
Forgetting to lowercase, so 'Aa' is reported as not a palindrome.
Allocating the cleaned copy when the interviewer asked for O(1) space.

approaches.name: Two Pointers — In-Place Skip (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'walk inward from both ends, skipping anything that isn't alphanumeric'.
hints: You don't actually need the cleaned string — you only need to compare matching positions. What if you tracked a left and a right index into the original string?
Move a left pointer rightward and a right pointer leftward. Before comparing, skip over any non-alphanumeric character on either side.
At each step, lowercase and compare s[l] with s[r]. If they differ, return false. Otherwise step both inward. Stop when l meets or passes r.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each pointer moves monotonically toward the other and never backtracks, so every index is visited at most once → O(n) time. Only two integer indices are stored → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Keep two indices: `l` at the start and `r` at the end. Repeatedly advance `l` past non-alphanumeric characters and retreat `r` past them, then compare the two alphanumeric characters case-insensitively. If they ever differ, it's not a palindrome; otherwise step both inward and continue until the pointers meet.

**The mental shift that unlocks this.** The brute force allocates a cleaned string just so it can compare position `i` with position `n−1−i`. But those positions already exist in the original string — we only need a way to *skip the junk between them*. Two pointers do exactly that without ever materializing a second buffer.

**Why the inner skip loops need the `l < r` guard.** Imagine a string that is all punctuation, like ",.;". The left pointer keeps advancing looking for an alphanumeric character and would run off the end of the string. Guarding each inner `while` with `l < r` stops the skip the instant the pointers meet, so we never index out of bounds and an all-symbol string correctly returns true.

**Why lowercasing both sides matters.** The comparison is case-insensitive, so 'A' at the left must match 'a' at the right. Lowercasing (or uppercasing) both characters right before the comparison handles that uniformly — forgetting it makes "Aa" report as a non-palindrome.

**Why this is O(1) space.** We never build a new string. The only state is two integer indices, regardless of input size. That's the entire reason to prefer this over clean-and-compare.
approaches.insight: Two pointers turn 'compare the string to its reverse' into 'compare the i-th and (n−1−i)-th meaningful characters as we go' — same comparison, no buffer. The in-place skip is the reusable trick: whenever you'd build a filtered copy only to scan it, ask whether two indices into the original can do the job.

edgeCases.behavior: Single space is non-alnum; both skip loops collapse l and r to the same spot, loop never compares → return true.

pitfalls: Dropping the inner `l < r` guard — pointers run off the ends on all-symbol strings and crash.
Using `isLetter` instead of `isLetterOrDigit` — silently treats digits as junk.

commonMistakes: Filtering only letters and forgetting digits count as alphanumeric.
Comparing characters without normalizing case first.
Removing the `l < r` guard inside the skip loops, causing index-out-of-bounds on all-symbol input.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping only letters, not digits
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 'Alphanumeric' includes 0-9. Filtering with isLetter drops digits, so "121" loses its digits and the logic breaks.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the l < r guard in the skip loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On an all-symbol string the skip loop keeps advancing and indexes past the end of the string, throwing an exception.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while not s[l].isalnum():
    l += 1   # runs off the end if no alnum chars remain
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while l < r and not s[l].isalnum():
    l += 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting case-insensitivity
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Comparing raw characters makes 'A' != 'a', so palindromes with mixed case are wrongly rejected.
